title: Robotics Careers and Honest Timelines
short: Most robotics engineers hold an engineering degree; technicians often start with two years of training. A portfolio of finished projects helps at every level.
trouble: Learners believe a six-month course alone leads to an engineering job title.

blocks.html: Robotics jobs are real and interesting, and the path to them is well known. Here is what the official numbers say, without hype.

"Robotics engineer" is not its own category in U.S. government job data. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) counts robotic engineers among mechanical engineers; many others work as electrical and electronics engineers, software developers, or electro-mechanical and mechatronics technicians. Engineering jobs typically start with a bachelor's degree; technician jobs with an associate's degree or a certificate.

blocks.html: Short online roadmaps can build real skills and a portfolio, and that matters at every level. But a few months of self-study is not the same as an engineering degree, and employers know it. An honest plan uses self-study to explore, to build projects, and to prepare for a technician program, a degree, or a robotics-related software role.

items: Middle and high school: FIRST LEGO League, FIRST Tech Challenge and FIRST Robotics Competition; math through precalculus, and calculus if you can; physics.
Two-year path: a community college program in mechatronics, electronics or automation leads to technician work that keeps robots running in factories and warehouses.
Four-year path: a bachelor's in mechanical, electrical or computer engineering, or computer science, with robotics electives, a robotics club and internships.
Career changers: people with software or technician experience often move in through robotics software or test roles, building on what they know.

blocks.title: Hours
blocks.q: Ten hours a week for 26 weeks.
blocks.a: 260 hours: about two college courses' worth of work.
